author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.biography: Dostoevsky survived a staged execution, years of penal servitude and recurring financial distress. He returned to literature with an intense interest in what ideas become when people have to live them, especially under the pressure of guilt, pride, affection and faith. Dostoevsky returned throughout his life to faith, freedom and responsibility. His final novel gives these questions a household in which intellectual arguments and family injuries cannot be kept apart.

hook.text: Could you forgive the world for what it does to the innocent?

paragraphs: The Karamazovs are a family with unfinished business. Their father is selfish and provocative; his sons meet him with different mixtures of need, contempt, rivalry and longing. Arguments about money and love quickly become arguments about what people owe one another.

Dostoevsky gives those disputes an enormous reach. One brother presses on the suffering of the innocent. Another tries to live through faith and active care. Desire and resentment keep upsetting everyone's account of what they believe. A position that sounds convincing in conversation becomes harder to maintain when somebody is crying in the next room.

The novel's power lies in allowing its strongest objections to remain strong. Faith must face cruelty; freedom must face responsibility; love must do more than admire humanity from a distance. Nobody gets to settle the problem merely by sounding intelligent.
Read the family drama with the same attention as the famous speeches. When we say that the world ought to be different, what follows for the person who is standing immediately in front of us?

orientation.text: The central brothers are Dmitri, Ivan and Alexei, usually called Alyosha. Their patronymics and nicknames vary; follow the family relationships before the philosophical debates.
